where Ω\Omega is the environment state space, 𝒪\mathcal{O} is the observation space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action or output space, 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the state transition mechanism, ℱ\mathcal{F} is the feedback generation mechanism, and 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the rule that converts feedback into optimization signals. Importantly, the notion of environment is understood here in a broad sense: it includes not only the external world, but also the data distribution presented to the model, task formats, supervision protocols, and even the loss rules by which feedback is transformed into gradients.

Let the model be denoted by MθM_{\theta}, with internal state space ℋ\mathcal{H}, state update map UθU_{\theta}, and policy or generation map Πθ\Pi_{\theta}. At interaction step tt, the closed-loop system can be written as

ot\displaystyle o_{t} ∼Pℰ(⋅∣ωt),\displaystyle\sim P_{\mathcal{E}}(\cdot\mid\omega_{t}), (8.2)
ht\displaystyle h_{t} =Uθ​(ht−1,ot),\displaystyle=U_{\theta}(h_{t-1},o_{t}), (8.3)
at\displaystyle a_{t} ∼Πθ(⋅∣ht),\displaystyle\sim\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t}), (8.4)
ξt\displaystyle\xi_{t} ∼ℱ(⋅∣ωt,ot,at),\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{F}(\cdot\mid\omega_{t},o_{t},a_{t}), (8.5)
ωt+1\displaystyle\omega_{t+1} ∼𝒯(⋅∣ωt,ot,at,ξt),\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{T}(\cdot\mid\omega_{t},o_{t},a_{t},\xi_{t}), (8.6)
ℓt\displaystyle\ell_{t} =𝒢​(ωt,ot,at,ξt).\displaystyle=\mathcal{G}(\omega_{t},o_{t},a_{t},\xi_{t}). (8.7)

The overall learning objective is therefore

𝒥​(θ;ℰ)=𝔼τ∼P​(τ∣θ,ℰ)​[∑t=1Tγt−1​ℓt],\mathcal{J}(\theta;\mathcal{E})=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim P(\tau\mid\theta,\mathcal{E})}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{t-1}\ell_{t}\right], (8.8)

where τ\tau denotes a complete interaction trajectory and γ\gamma is the discount factor.

This formalization shows directly that learning is never an isolated question of model structure alone. Rather, it is jointly determined by three factors: first, the state space in which the model absorbs and organizes information; second, the kind of feedback through which the environment defines improvement; and third, the actual structure that generates observations, transitions, and feedback. In this work, these three aspects correspond precisely to the three recurring themes of the paper: how text should be represented, which metrics are aligned with the true learning objective, and what kind of environment unified models are ultimately meant to enter.

8.1 Rethinking Text Modeling Paradigms: From State Space in the System to Hierarchical Text Generation

From a system-level perspective, the central question of text modeling is not merely which generation order to adopt, but rather in what kind of state text should be represented within the learning system. Mainstream autoregressive language models bind the state tightly to the surface token prefix, and generation is therefore written as

pAR​(x)=∏t=1npθ​(xt∣x<t).p_{\mathrm{AR}}(x)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}p_{\theta}(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}). (8.9)

This factorization is highly effective, but it fundamentally corresponds to a strong modeling assumption: both global semantics and local realization are propagated through the same token-level conditional chain. In other words, it assumes that the surface string itself is the most natural and primary state space.

The route explored in this paper instead reconsiders text generation from the level of the state space itself. If text indeed contains a low-dimensional yet sufficiently useful global semantic structure, then a more natural approach is not to place the entire burden of generation on a token-level chain factorization, but to introduce latent variables explicitly and model high-level semantic organization separately from local textual realization. Correspondingly, the core factorization of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is

p​(x,z0)=pθ​(x∣z0)​pψ​(z0),p​(x)=∫pθ​(x∣z0)​pψ​(z0)​𝑑z0,p(x,z_{0})=p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})p_{\psi}(z_{0}),\qquad p(x)=\int p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})p_{\psi}(z_{0})\,dz_{0}, (8.10)

where z0z_{0} is a continuous latent variable, pψ​(z0)p_{\psi}(z_{0}) is the latent prior, and pθ​(x∣z0)p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}) is the conditional decoder. The crucial change here is not merely the introduction of latent variables, but the redefinition of the role of state in the system: the path no longer acts directly on observation recovery, but instead organizes global semantics in latent space first, after which the decoder carries out local textual realization.

This point can be stated compactly through the information decomposition of the average ELBO. Let

q​(x,z0):=pdata​(x)​qϕ​(z0∣x),q(x,z_{0}):=p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x), (8.11)

then

𝔼pdata​(x)​[ℒELBO​(x)]=𝔼q​(x,z0)​[log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)]−Iq​(X;Z0)−KL​(q¯ϕ​(z0)∥pψ​(z0)),\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)]=\mathbb{E}_{q(x,z_{0})}[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})]-I_{q}(X;Z_{0})-\mathrm{KL}\!\big(\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0})\,\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{0})\big), (8.12)

where q¯ϕ​(z0)\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0}) is the aggregated posterior. This decomposition shows that hierarchical latent-space modeling breaks the text problem into three coupled but analytically distinguishable components: conditional realization, information compression, and prior matching. The latent variable is therefore not merely a continuous surrogate for discrete tokens, but an explicit intermediate state through which global semantic organization can be separated from local textual realization and modeled on its own terms.

From this perspective, compression must also be reconsidered. Prior work has emphasized the connection between compression and intelligence [37], while recent explorations of generation closer to raw data forms in images and videos, such as pixel-space modeling [19], further suggest that compression should not be equated with harmful information deletion. The key question is not whether every local detail is preserved, but whether the model can extract and organize structural information that is genuinely effective and generalizable. If text indeed admits a hierarchical structure in which high-level semantics and low-level realization are relatively separable, then reinterpreting text generation through informational hierarchy is not merely a change of method, but a theoretical re-evaluation of text modeling itself.

Accordingly, the first theme of this paper is not to reject autoregression, but to point out that autoregression occupies only one self-consistent, rather than unique, corner of the design space. If the data truly contains a hierarchy between low-dimensional global semantics and high-dimensional local realization, then organizing semantics first in a latent state and realizing text through conditional decoding may be closer to the true generative mechanism. Text generation should therefore not be understood solely as next-token fitting over discrete strings, but more generally as a systematic problem of how information is represented, compressed, and organized hierarchically.

8.2 Understanding the Continuous Extension of Discrete Text: From Objective Mismatch to a Shift in Evaluation Emphasis

Once the state space of the system is changed, the issue at the objective level changes accordingly. For conventional autoregressive language models, the training objective and evaluation quantities are naturally well aligned: maximum likelihood training directly corresponds to probability fitting over text, and likelihood and perplexity therefore have a clear and stable interpretation. In hierarchical continuous latent-space models, however, the actual training path is no longer direct token-level maximum likelihood, but a hierarchical objective jointly composed of reconstruction, latent prior learning, and representation regularization.

This can be seen from the relation between the ELBO and the true marginal likelihood:

−ℒELBO(x)=−logpθ,ψ(x)+KL(qϕ(z0∣x)∥pθ,ψ(z0∣x)).-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)=-\log p_{\theta,\psi}(x)+\mathrm{KL}\!\big(q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\,\|\,p_{\theta,\psi}(z_{0}\mid x)\big). (8.13)

This shows that even at the level of the ELBO, the training objective is already separated from the true log-likelihood by a variational inference gap. Furthermore, in the actual training of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM, the model must jointly learn latent reconstruction, continuous prior fitting, and representation stabilization. The quantity being optimized is therefore not a single token-level likelihood in the classical sense.

For this reason, the mismatch should not be interpreted as a failure to learn, but rather as evidence that the model is learning something different. For autoregressive models and other paradigms that directly fit discrete distributions, likelihood and perplexity remain highly informative because they are naturally aligned with the training objective. For hierarchical continuous latent-space models, by contrast, the central issue is no longer whether local discrete distributions are fitted as sharply as possible, but whether higher-level semantic structures are effectively organized, whether the latent prior is well learned, and whether the final generations satisfy the actual task requirements.

From the perspective of systematic modeling, this phenomenon is in fact expected: when the state space expands from surface tokens to hierarchical latent variables, the optimization target correspondingly shifts from precise fitting of local discrete distributions to the organization of higher-level semantic structure, stable latent prior learning, and satisfaction of the true generative objective. For this route, generation-oriented metrics are therefore often more closely aligned with what the model is actually trained to do than perplexity. More importantly, model potential is often reflected more clearly in scaling behavior than in any single static likelihood value: what matters is whether capability continues to improve steadily as model size, data, and compute increase, rather than whether local fit under a particular pointwise metric is better.

This can also be connected to the perspective of the three governing curves developed in the theoretical analysis of the paper. For 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM, the applicability of this route is not determined by a single likelihood value, but by whether three conditions hold simultaneously: the representation rate–distortion curve is already favorable at relatively low rate, the approximation error of the latent prior continues to decrease, and the inference gap remains controllable. In other words, the advantage of this route is not guaranteed automatically by latent variables or flow-based modeling themselves; it depends on whether the data truly contains a compressible global semantic structure, and whether the model can learn, fit, and realize that structure in a stable manner.

The second theme of this paper is therefore not merely that perplexity is inadequate, but that evaluation language itself must change once representation and objective have changed. For this class of models, generation quality and scaling behavior are often closer to the model’s true capability and long-term potential than traditional perplexity.

8.3 Exploring Unified Models: Model-Environment Interaction and the Value of Multimodal Unification

If we return again to the model–environment formalization in Eq. (8.1) and Eq. (8.8), the third theme becomes more natural. The importance of unified models does not lie merely in placing multiple modalities within a single parameterized network, but in changing the structure of the environment in which the model learns. In the real world, observations, transitions, and feedback are usually not generated independently across modalities; rather, they are often jointly determined by a shared latent state. A more general learning system therefore requires not a set of isolated modality interfaces placed side by side, but unified representations that can enter the same interaction state and share the same dynamical constraints.

This is closely related to two broader views of intelligence. One influential view understands intelligence as a collection of skills across tasks [16]. Under this view, a system becomes more capable because it can solve problems across more domains and under more diverse forms of supervision and interaction. The recent development of large language models partly reflects this tendency. A representative example is the progress of code agents that can operate within command-line environments. In such environments, the observation space, action space, and feedback mechanism are unusually well aligned with discrete symbolic representations. Interaction trajectories are easy to record, and correctness is often straightforward to verify, so these environments provide dense and precise learning signals.

Another view, closer to the world-model perspective, holds that intelligence consists in acquiring an internal model of the structure and dynamics of the world. Recent work on world models [93] moves in this direction by seeking to learn richer environmental dynamics, thereby supporting stronger generalization and more realistic interaction. From this perspective, the question is not only how many tasks a model can solve, but whether it learns in an environment whose structure is rich enough to induce the right abstractions. The environment therefore becomes central: a model can only internalize the regularities that are actually present in the observations, transitions, and feedback it encounters.

This can also be written more formally. Let the observation at step tt be multimodal,

ot=(ot(1),ot(2),…,ot(M)),ot(m)∈𝒪(m),o_{t}=\big(o_{t}^{(1)},o_{t}^{(2)},\dots,o_{t}^{(M)}\big),\qquad o_{t}^{(m)}\in\mathcal{O}^{(m)}, (8.14)

and suppose there exists a joint latent state

zt=Φ​(ot(1),…,ot(M)),z_{t}=\Phi\!\left(o_{t}^{(1)},\dots,o_{t}^{(M)}\right), (8.15)

such that feedback and transition depend primarily on this joint state rather than on marginal factorizations over modalities:

ξt,ωt+1∼p​(ξt,ωt+1∣zt,at).\xi_{t},\omega_{t+1}\sim p\big(\xi_{t},\omega_{t+1}\mid z_{t},a_{t}\big). (8.16)

If the true environmental dynamics satisfy

p​(ξt,ωt+1∣ot,at)≠∏m=1Mpm​(ξt(m),ωt+1(m)∣ot(m),at(m)),p(\xi_{t},\omega_{t+1}\mid o_{t},a_{t})\neq\prod_{m=1}^{M}p_{m}\big(\xi_{t}^{(m)},\omega_{t+1}^{(m)}\mid o_{t}^{(m)},a_{t}^{(m)}\big), (8.17)

then the learning problem is structurally non-separable across modalities. In such a case, treating each modality as an independent channel and only combining them superficially is generally insufficient. The theoretical significance of unified models lies precisely in the fact that the environment itself is non-separable in the sense of Eq. (8.17): the regularities that determine useful feedback are joint regularities rather than regularities defined on the marginal distribution of each modality.

This clarifies why multimodal unification is not merely an engineering convenience. Its purpose is not simply to process multiple data types with one backbone, but to allow the model to learn in an environment whose observation, transition, and supervision structure more faithfully reflects the coupled regularities of the real world. In such an environment, both inputs and outputs may be multimodal; useful feedback may depend on how different modalities constrain each other jointly; and the learned internal state should ideally reflect these joint constraints.

This also explains why text has long been the most difficult component in unified models. Images and videos naturally operate in continuous spaces, whereas text is a prototypically discrete modality. If they are to enter a common interaction state and share latent dynamics, a severe representational mismatch immediately arises. This is precisely one of the central obstacles repeatedly identified in recent unified-model research [18]. In this sense, the significance of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM lies not only in proposing another text generator, but in providing a natural interface through which discrete text can enter a continuous latent space.

If discrete text is mapped into a continuous latent variable through

ztext∼qϕ​(z∣xtext),xtext∼pη​(x∣ztext),z^{\mathrm{text}}\sim q_{\phi}(z\mid x^{\mathrm{text}}),\qquad x^{\mathrm{text}}\sim p_{\eta}(x\mid z^{\mathrm{text}}), (8.18)

then text acquires an interface compatible with other continuous modalities. One may then define a unified interaction state

z~t=Ψ​(zttext,ztimg,ztvid,…),\tilde{z}_{t}=\Psi\!\left(z_{t}^{\mathrm{text}},z_{t}^{\mathrm{img}},z_{t}^{\mathrm{vid}},\dots\right), (8.19)

and perform state evolution, decision making, and feedback modeling at this level. Equations (8.18)–(8.19) formalize why 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM may matter beyond text generation itself: its role is not only to generate text through a different path, but to provide a bridge through which an intrinsically discrete modality can participate in a continuous multimodal interaction state. In other words, it reduces the structural mismatch that otherwise prevents text from naturally entering a shared continuous environment.

This is why the broader significance of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is better understood through model–environment interaction than through single-modality benchmarks alone. If learning is viewed as the optimization of Eq. (8.8) in richer and more realistic environments, then unified models matter because they expand the environments in which the model can learn. If text is to participate fully in such environments, then a bridge such as that in Eq. (8.18) becomes especially desirable. In this sense, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is not merely an alternative text generator; it can also be understood as a candidate mechanism for aligning discrete text with continuous multimodal learning systems.

8.4 The Three Themes Under a Unified Perspective

In summary, the three themes of this paper are not separate supplementary discussions, but three manifestations of the same systematic problem. The first concerns the representation level: whether text should be modeled entirely on the token surface, or whether higher-level semantics can be organized in an independent latent state. The second concerns the objective level: once the model is trained through latent transport, reconstruction, and regularization rather than direct token-level maximum likelihood, which metrics remain genuinely aligned with the learning problem. The third concerns the environment level: if learning is ultimately model–environment interaction, then what kind of environment future models should inhabit, and what representational interfaces are needed for different modalities to become compatible within it.

From this perspective, autoregressive language modeling occupies a self-consistent corner of the design space: representation is tightly bound to surface tokens, the training objective is direct likelihood maximization, and the environment is largely symbolic and text-centered. The route explored in this work changes all three assumptions simultaneously. It introduces a hierarchical latent-variable representation for text, thereby changing the representational assumption; it moves optimization away from direct token-level likelihood, thereby weakening the central interpretive role of perplexity; and it provides a continuous interface for discrete text, thereby making text potentially more compatible with multimodal environments that are more naturally expressed in continuous latent space.

We therefore hope that the contribution of this work is not only a viable alternative path for text generation, but also a more systematic way of thinking that jointly considers representation, objective alignment, and environment design. More broadly, we hope it encourages future research to rethink text, images, videos, and other modalities not as isolated domains that must be solved separately, but as components of a larger learning system in which unified representation, unified objectives, and unified environments may become increasingly central to the development of more general multimodal intelligence.

\beginappendix

9 Strict Probabilistic Formulation and Training Objective Details of Cola DLM

This appendix provides the strict probabilistic formulation of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM and clarifies the role of each training component. We first define the latent-variable model and the CNF prior precisely, then derive the marginal likelihood, the ELBO, and its population form, and finally explain the exact role of Flow Matching in the overall theoretical framework.

9.1 Probabilistic Objects, CNF Prior, and Generative Distribution

Let x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} denote a discrete text sequence, and let z0∈ℝdz_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote its continuous latent variable. 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM consists of three probabilistic components:

qϕ​(z0∣x)\displaystyle q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x) encoder (approximate posterior),\displaystyle\quad\text{encoder (approximate posterior)}, (9.1)
pθ​(x∣z0)\displaystyle p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}) decoder (conditional text generator),\displaystyle\quad\text{decoder (conditional text generator)}, (9.2)
pψ​(z0)\displaystyle p_{\psi}(z_{0}) latent prior (defined by a continuous flow).\displaystyle\quad\text{latent prior (defined by a continuous flow)}. (9.3)

Here, qϕ​(z0∣x)q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x) is used only for variational inference during training. The actual generative distribution is defined by pθ​(x∣z0)p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}) and pψ​(z0)p_{\psi}(z_{0}).

To ensure that the flow map and density-transport formula are well defined, we impose the standard regularity assumption on the CNF vector field.

Assumption 9.1 (Regularity of the CNF vector field).

For each parameter ψ\psi, the vector field 𝒗ψ​(z,t)\bm{v}_{\psi}(z,t) is locally Lipschitz in zz, measurable in tt, and satisfies a linear-growth condition ensuring the existence and uniqueness of global ODE solutions. In addition, ∇⋅𝒗ψ​(z,t)\nabla\!\cdot\bm{v}_{\psi}(z,t) is integrable along the trajectories of interest. Then, for any 0≤s≤t≤10\leq s\leq t\leq 1, the flow map Φt←sψ\Phi^{\psi}_{t\leftarrow s} exists, is unique, and is invertible.

Let the base distribution be the standard Gaussian

z1∼p1​(z1)=𝒩​(0,I).z_{1}\sim p_{1}(z_{1})=\mathcal{N}(0,I). (9.4)

Given a time-dependent vector field 𝒗ψ​(zt,t)\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t), consider the ODE

d​ztd​t=𝒗ψ​(zt,t),t∈[0,1].\frac{\mathrm{d}z_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t),\qquad t\in[0,1]. (9.5)

By Assumption 9.1, this ODE induces a flow map

zt=Φt←sψ​(zs).z_{t}=\Phi^{\psi}_{t\leftarrow s}(z_{s}). (9.6)

Therefore, a prior sample can be written as

z0=Φ0←1ψ​(z1),z1∼p1.z_{0}=\Phi^{\psi}_{0\leftarrow 1}(z_{1}),\qquad z_{1}\sim p_{1}. (9.7)

Equivalently, the prior distribution is the pushforward of the base distribution under the reverse flow:

pψ=(Φ0←1ψ)♯​p1.p_{\psi}=(\Phi^{\psi}_{0\leftarrow 1})_{\sharp}p_{1}. (9.8)

This shows that pψ​(z0)p_{\psi}(z_{0}) is not an abstract symbol, but a rigorously defined probability distribution induced jointly by (p1,𝒗ψ)(p_{1},\bm{v}_{\psi}).

Hence, the generative process of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM can be written as

z1∼p1​(z1),z0=Φ0←1ψ​(z1),x∼pθ​(x∣z0).z_{1}\sim p_{1}(z_{1}),\qquad z_{0}=\Phi^{\psi}_{0\leftarrow 1}(z_{1}),\qquad x\sim p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}). (9.9)

The corresponding joint and marginal distributions are

p​(x,z0)=pθ​(x∣z0)​pψ​(z0),p​(x)=∫pθ​(x∣z0)​pψ​(z0)​dz0.p(x,z_{0})=p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})p_{\psi}(z_{0}),\qquad p(x)=\int p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})p_{\psi}(z_{0})\,\mathrm{d}z_{0}. (9.10)

If the base variable z1z_{1} is introduced explicitly, the marginal can also be written as

p​(x)=∫p1​(z1)​pθ​(x∣Φ0←1ψ​(z1))​dz1.p(x)=\int p_{1}(z_{1})\,p_{\theta}\bigl(x\mid\Phi^{\psi}_{0\leftarrow 1}(z_{1})\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}z_{1}. (9.11)

Therefore, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is fundamentally a hierarchical latent-variable language model, rather than a model that directly defines a reverse process in token space.

9.2 Explicit Density of the CNF Prior and the Outer ELBO

Let ZtZ_{t} denote the random variable induced by the ODE at time tt, with density ptp_{t}. Under Assumption 9.1, ptp_{t} satisfies the continuity equation

∂tpt​(z)+∇⋅(pt​(z)​𝒗ψ​(z,t))=0.\partial_{t}p_{t}(z)+\nabla\!\cdot\bigl(p_{t}(z)\,\bm{v}_{\psi}(z,t)\bigr)=0.

Along a characteristic trajectory t↦ztt\mapsto z_{t}, the instantaneous change-of-variables formula gives

dd​t​log⁡pt​(zt)=−∇⋅𝒗ψ​(zt,t).\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\log p_{t}(z_{t})=-\nabla\!\cdot\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t). (9.12)

Integrating from 0 to 11, and noting that p0=pψp_{0}=p_{\psi}, yields

log⁡pψ​(z0)=log⁡p1​(z1)+∫01∇⋅𝒗ψ​(zt,t)​dt,z1=Φ1←0ψ​(z0).\log p_{\psi}(z_{0})=\log p_{1}(z_{1})+\int_{0}^{1}\nabla\!\cdot\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t)\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad z_{1}=\Phi^{\psi}_{1\leftarrow 0}(z_{0}). (9.13)

Thus, the CNF prior admits an explicitly defined log-density rather than an implicit prior that exists only through sampling.

The flow map can also be written as a deterministic Markov kernel. Define

Kt←sψ​(d​zt∣zs):=δΦt←sψ​(zs)​(d​zt).K^{\psi}_{t\leftarrow s}(\mathrm{d}z_{t}\mid z_{s}):=\delta_{\Phi^{\psi}_{t\leftarrow s}(z_{s})}(\mathrm{d}z_{t}). (9.14)

By the semigroup property of ODE flows, Kt←sψK^{\psi}_{t\leftarrow s} satisfies the Chapman–Kolmogorov relation and therefore forms a deterministic Markov semigroup. However, the Markov structure here comes from prior transport, not from an observation-dependent corruption–recovery mechanism.

We now introduce the variational posterior qϕ​(z0∣x)q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x) to handle the latent integral in the marginal likelihood. For any qϕ​(z0∣x)q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x) satisfying the required support condition,

log⁡p​(x)\displaystyle\log p(x) =log​∫qϕ​(z0∣x)​pθ​(x∣z0)​pψ​(z0)qϕ​(z0∣x)​dz0\displaystyle=\log\int q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\frac{p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})p_{\psi}(z_{0})}{q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)}\,\mathrm{d}z_{0} (9.15)
≥𝔼qϕ​(z0∣x)​[log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)+log⁡pψ​(z0)−log⁡qϕ​(z0∣x)].\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)}\Bigl[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})+\log p_{\psi}(z_{0})-\log q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\Bigr]. (9.16)

Define the outer ELBO as

ℒELBO​(x):=𝔼qϕ​(z0∣x)​[log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)+log⁡pψ​(z0)−log⁡qϕ​(z0∣x)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)}\Bigl[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})+\log p_{\psi}(z_{0})-\log q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\Bigr]. (9.17)

Then

log⁡p​(x)≥ℒELBO​(x).\log p(x)\geq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x). (9.18)

More importantly, the exact decomposition between the true log-likelihood and the ELBO is

logp(x)=ℒELBO(x)+KL(qϕ(z0∣x)∥p(z0∣x)),\log p(x)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)+\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\,\|\,p(z_{0}\mid x)\bigr), (9.19)

where the true posterior is

p​(z0∣x)=pθ​(x∣z0)​pψ​(z0)p​(x).p(z_{0}\mid x)=\frac{p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})p_{\psi}(z_{0})}{p(x)}. (9.20)

Equation (9.19) makes the distinction explicit: the true likelihood is always log⁡p​(x)\log p(x), whereas the training objective directly optimized is its variational lower bound ℒELBO​(x)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x).

Substituting the explicit CNF density formula (9.13) into the outer ELBO gives

ℒELBO(x)=𝔼qϕ​(z0∣x)[\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)}\Bigl[ log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)+log⁡p1​(z1)+∫01∇⋅𝒗ψ​(zt,t)​dt\displaystyle\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})+\log p_{1}(z_{1})+\int_{0}^{1}\nabla\!\cdot\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t)\,\mathrm{d}t (9.21)
−logqϕ(z0∣x)],z1=Φψ1←0(z0).\displaystyle-\log q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\Bigr],\qquad z_{1}=\Phi^{\psi}_{1\leftarrow 0}(z_{0}). (9.22)

This is the strict training objective of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM in the setting where the decoder can compute log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}).

9.3 Average ELBO, Aggregated Posterior, and Prior Matching

To analyze the nature of prior learning, define the aggregated posterior

q¯ϕ​(z0):=∫qϕ​(z0∣x)​pdata​(x)​dx,\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0}):=\int q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x, (9.23)

and the joint distribution

q​(x,z0):=pdata​(x)​qϕ​(z0∣x).q(x,z_{0}):=p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x). (9.24)

When the encoder qϕq_{\phi} and decoder pθp_{\theta} are fixed, the dependence of the data-averaged ELBO on ψ\psi appears only through the prior term:

𝔼pdata​(x)​[ℒELBO​(x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)\bigr] =𝔼q​(x,z0)​[log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)−log⁡qϕ​(z0∣x)]+𝔼q​(x,z0)​[log⁡pψ​(z0)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q(x,z_{0})}\bigl[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})-\log q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\bigr]+\mathbb{E}_{q(x,z_{0})}\bigl[\log p_{\psi}(z_{0})\bigr] (9.25)
=C​(ϕ,θ)+𝔼z0∼q¯ϕ​[log⁡pψ​(z0)],\displaystyle=C(\phi,\theta)+\mathbb{E}_{z_{0}\sim\bar{q}_{\phi}}\bigl[\log p_{\psi}(z_{0})\bigr], (9.26)

where C​(ϕ,θ)C(\phi,\theta) is independent of ψ\psi.

Using

𝔼z0∼q¯ϕ​[log⁡pψ​(z0)]=−KL​(q¯ϕ​(z0)∥pψ​(z0))+𝔼z0∼q¯ϕ​[log⁡q¯ϕ​(z0)],\mathbb{E}_{z_{0}\sim\bar{q}_{\phi}}[\log p_{\psi}(z_{0})]=-\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0})\,\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{0})\bigr)+\mathbb{E}_{z_{0}\sim\bar{q}_{\phi}}[\log\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0})],

we obtain

maxψ⁡𝔼pdata​(x)​[ℒELBO​(x)]⟺minψ⁡KL​(q¯ϕ​(z0)∥pψ​(z0)).\max_{\psi}\;\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)\bigr]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\min_{\psi}\;\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0})\,\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{0})\bigr). (9.27)

Therefore, after fixing the encoder and decoder, the strict prior-learning subproblem is to fit the aggregated posterior q¯ϕ\bar{q}_{\phi} with pψp_{\psi}.

The average ELBO can be further written in information-decomposition form. Adding and subtracting log⁡q¯ϕ​(z0)\log\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0}) in the prior term yields

𝔼pdata​(x)​[ℒELBO​(x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)] =𝔼q​(x,z0)​[log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)]−Iq​(X;Z0)−KL​(q¯ϕ​(z0)∥pψ​(z0)),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q(x,z_{0})}[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})]-I_{q}(X;Z_{0})-\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0})\,\|\,p_{\psi}(z_{0})\bigr), (9.28)

where

Iq​(X;Z0):=𝔼pdata​(x)​[KL​(qϕ​(z0∣x)∥q¯ϕ​(z0))]I_{q}(X;Z_{0}):=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}\Bigl[\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\,\|\,\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0})\bigr)\Bigr] (9.29)

is the amount of information retained in the latent variable.

Equation (9.28) reveals the three theoretical roles of the encoder. It determines the target distribution q¯ϕ​(z0)\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0}) that the prior must fit, the compression strength through Iq​(X;Z0)I_{q}(X;Z_{0}), and therefore the division of labor between global semantics in latent space and local realization in the decoder.

9.4 The Role of Flow Matching: A Prior Solver Rather Than the Model Definition

Direct optimization of log⁡pψ​(z0)\log p_{\psi}(z_{0}) usually requires repeated ODE solves and divergence estimation, which is expensive in practice. For this reason, Flow Matching is often used to learn the vector field of the same prior more efficiently. It should therefore be viewed as a prior solver, not as the likelihood objective itself.

To do so, one first specifies a bridge path from the aggregated posterior to the base distribution. Let

z0∼q¯ϕ​(z0),z1∼p1​(z1),t∼U​[0,1].z_{0}\sim\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0}),\qquad z_{1}\sim p_{1}(z_{1}),\qquad t\sim U[0,1]. (9.30)

Consider the conditional path

zt=(1−α​(t))​z0+α​(t)​z1,α​(0)=0,α​(1)=1.z_{t}=(1-\alpha(t))z_{0}+\alpha(t)z_{1},\qquad\alpha(0)=0,\ \alpha(1)=1. (9.31)

Here α\alpha can be any sufficiently smooth monotone function; linear interpolation corresponds to α​(t)=t\alpha(t)=t. The target velocity field of this path is

ut​(z0,z1):=d​ztd​t=α˙​(t)​(z1−z0).u_{t}(z_{0},z_{1}):=\frac{\mathrm{d}z_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\dot{\alpha}(t)(z_{1}-z_{0}). (9.32)

The Flow Matching loss is then

ℒFM​(ψ;ϕ):=𝔼t,z0∼q¯ϕ,z1∼p1​[‖𝒗ψ​(zt,t)−ut​(z0,z1)‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\psi;\phi):=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,z_{0}\sim\bar{q}_{\phi},\,z_{1}\sim p_{1}}\left[\left\|\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t)-u_{t}(z_{0},z_{1})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (9.33)

For a fixed path construction, the pointwise optimal solution is the conditional expectation

𝒗ψ⋆​(z,t)=𝔼​[ut​(z0,z1)∣zt=z,t].\bm{v}_{\psi}^{\star}(z,t)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[u_{t}(z_{0},z_{1})\mid z_{t}=z,\,t\bigr]. (9.34)

This is simply a conditional-mean regression result, but it makes the role of Flow Matching precise: under ideal conditions, the learned vector field corresponds to a continuous transport connecting q¯ϕ\bar{q}_{\phi} and p1p_{1}, which in turn defines the prior pψ​(z0)p_{\psi}(z_{0}).

Hence, two objectives must be distinguished. The first,

maxψ⁡𝔼z0∼q¯ϕ​[log⁡pψ​(z0)],\max_{\psi}\;\mathbb{E}_{z_{0}\sim\bar{q}_{\phi}}[\log p_{\psi}(z_{0})], (9.35)

is the strict probabilistic objective for prior learning. The second,

minψ⁡ℒFM​(ψ;ϕ),\min_{\psi}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\psi;\phi), (9.36)

is a practical solver for learning the vector field of the same prior. They serve the same prior-modeling problem, but they are not the same mathematical object. In particular, ℒFM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}} cannot be identified term-by-term with −log⁡pψ​(z0)-\log p_{\psi}(z_{0}) in the ELBO.

9.5 Strict Form of the Training Objective

If the decoder can compute log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}) exactly, then the strict training objective is to maximize (9.17), or equivalently to minimize the negative ELBO. Define

LREC​(x)\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{REC}}(x) :=−𝔼qϕ​(z0∣x)​[log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)],\displaystyle:=-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)}\bigl[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})\bigr], (9.37)
LPRIOR​(x)\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{PRIOR}}(x) :=−𝔼qϕ​(z0∣x)​[log⁡pψ​(z0)],\displaystyle:=-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)}\bigl[\log p_{\psi}(z_{0})\bigr], (9.38)
LREG​(x)\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{REG}}(x) :=𝔼qϕ​(z0∣x)​[log⁡qϕ​(z0∣x)],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)}\bigl[\log q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\bigr], (9.39)

so that the total single-sample loss becomes

LTotalstrict​(x):=LREC​(x)+LPRIOR​(x)+LREG​(x)=−ℒELBO​(x).L_{\mathrm{Total}}^{\mathrm{strict}}(x):=L_{\mathrm{REC}}(x)+L_{\mathrm{PRIOR}}(x)+L_{\mathrm{REG}}(x)=-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x). (9.40)

Taking expectation over the data distribution gives the strict training objective

minϕ,θ,ψ⁡𝔼pdata​(x)​[LTotalstrict​(x)]⟺maxϕ,θ,ψ⁡𝔼pdata​(x)​[ℒELBO​(x)].\min_{\phi,\theta,\psi}\;\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}\bigl[L_{\mathrm{Total}}^{\mathrm{strict}}(x)\bigr]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\max_{\phi,\theta,\psi}\;\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)\bigr]. (9.41)

Therefore, the objective that truly corresponds to maximizing a lower bound of the marginal likelihood is always the ELBO; Flow Matching is only an efficient implementation for learning the prior.

10 Sampling, Inference, and Probability Estimation Details

This appendix supplements the strict formulation of sampling, continuation, unconditional likelihood estimation, and conditional probability estimation in 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM. Since the main text only presents the overall framework, we provide the details here.

10.1 Sampling and Inference Procedure

To generate a new sample from 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM, one should follow the generative process defined by the model, rather than the approximate posterior path used during training. First, sample a latent seed from the simple base distribution:

z1∼p1​(z1)=𝒩​(0,I).z_{1}\sim p_{1}(z_{1})=\mathcal{N}(0,I). (10.1)

Second, integrate the vector field backward to obtain a latent sample:

d​ztd​t=𝒗ψ​(zt,t),t:1→0,\frac{\mathrm{d}z_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t),\qquad t:1\rightarrow 0, (10.2)

so that starting from z​(1)=z1z(1)=z_{1} yields z​(0)=z0z(0)=z_{0}. In practice, Euler, Heun, or higher-order ODE solvers can be used. This step generates global latent semantics rather than tokens themselves.

Third, the decoder generates text conditioned on the latent:

x∼pθ​(x∣z0).x\sim p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}). (10.3)

If the decoder is autoregressive, this step is conditional autoregressive sampling; if the decoder is non-autoregressive or bidirectional, it becomes the corresponding conditional recovery procedure. Hence, sampling in 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is inherently two-stage: one first samples a global latent, and then realizes the text conditioned on it.

If a task provides a prefix xprex^{\mathrm{pre}}, inference first encodes the prefix into a conditional latent:

zpre∼qϕ​(zpre∣xpre),z^{\mathrm{pre}}\sim q_{\phi}(z^{\mathrm{pre}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}}), (10.4)

and then generates the response latent block by block. Let the previously generated blocks be z^0(<b)\hat{z}_{0}^{(<b)}. The bb-th response block is generated by

z^0(b)=Φ0←1ψ​(ϵ(b);zpre,z^0(<b)),ϵ(b)∼𝒩​(0,I).\hat{z}_{0}^{(b)}=\Phi^{\psi}_{0\leftarrow 1}\!\bigl(\epsilon^{(b)};z^{\mathrm{pre}},\hat{z}_{0}^{(<b)}\bigr),\qquad\epsilon^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (10.5)

The response is then decoded as

x^res∼pθ​(xres∣xpre,zpre,z^0(1:B)).\hat{x}^{\mathrm{res}}\sim p_{\theta}\!\bigl(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}},z^{\mathrm{pre}},\hat{z}_{0}^{(1:B)}\bigr). (10.6)

This is exactly the prefix-encoding, blockwise-generation, and conditional-decoding procedure described in the main text.

10.2 Unconditional Log-Likelihood and PPL Estimation

For a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, if one directly uses the ELBO as a lower bound on log⁡p​(x)\log p(x), one may define an ELBO-based perplexity as

PPLELBO:=exp⁡(−∑x∈𝒟ℒELBO​(x)∑x∈𝒟|x|),\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}:=\exp\left(-\frac{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)}{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}}|x|}\right), (10.7)

where |x||x| denotes sequence length. Since ℒELBO​(x)≤log⁡p​(x)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)\leq\log p(x), PPLELBO\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{ELBO}} should be interpreted as an upper-bound-type estimate of the true perplexity.

If the decoder can compute log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}), one can also obtain tighter likelihood estimates through importance sampling or IWAE. Let

z0(k)∼qϕ​(z0∣x),log⁡w(k)=log⁡pθ​(x∣z0(k))+log⁡pψ​(z0(k))−log⁡qϕ​(z0(k)∣x).z_{0}^{(k)}\sim q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x),\qquad\log w^{(k)}=\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}^{(k)})+\log p_{\psi}(z_{0}^{(k)})-\log q_{\phi}(z_{0}^{(k)}\mid x). (10.8)

Then the ELBO-style and IWAE-style estimators are

log⁡p^ELBO,K​(x)=1K​∑k=1Klog⁡w(k),log⁡p^IWAE,K​(x)=log⁡(1K​∑k=1Kelog⁡w(k)).\log\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{ELBO},K}(x)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log w^{(k)},\qquad\log\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{IWAE},K}(x)=\log\!\left(\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}e^{\log w^{(k)}}\right). (10.9)

The IWAE estimator is generally tighter. When IWAE is used for scoring, the corresponding perplexity is

PPLIWAE:=exp⁡(−∑x∈𝒟log⁡p^IWAE,K​(x)∑x∈𝒟|x|).\mathrm{PPL}_{\mathrm{IWAE}}:=\exp\left(-\frac{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}}\log\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{IWAE},K}(x)}{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}}|x|}\right). (10.10)

If the decoder itself can provide only a lower bound, then evaluation can report only bound-based PPL rather than exact perplexity.

10.3 Conditional Probability Estimation and Block-Level Conditional Scoring

In continuation, multiple-choice evaluation, and candidate-response ranking, conditional probability is more important than the unconditional score. Let a full sample be decomposed as

x=(xpre,xres),x=(x^{\mathrm{pre}},x^{\mathrm{res}}), (10.11)

where xprex^{\mathrm{pre}} is the given prefix and xresx^{\mathrm{res}} is the response to be evaluated. The exact conditional log-probability satisfies

log⁡p​(xres∣xpre)=log⁡p​(xpre,xres)−log⁡p​(xpre).\log p(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}})=\log p(x^{\mathrm{pre}},x^{\mathrm{res}})-\log p(x^{\mathrm{pre}}). (10.12)

Hence one can apply the same unconditional estimator separately to the joint sample and the prefix sample, and then take the difference to obtain a plug-in conditional estimator:

log⁡p^condELBO​(xres∣xpre):=ℒELBO​(xpre,xres)−ℒELBO​(xpre),\widehat{\log p}_{\mathrm{cond}}^{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}}):=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x^{\mathrm{pre}},x^{\mathrm{res}})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x^{\mathrm{pre}}), (10.13)

and

log⁡p^cond,KIWAE​(xres∣xpre):=log⁡p^IWAE,K​(xpre,xres)−log⁡p^IWAE,K​(xpre).\widehat{\log p}_{\mathrm{cond},K}^{\mathrm{IWAE}}(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}}):=\log\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{IWAE},K}(x^{\mathrm{pre}},x^{\mathrm{res}})-\log\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{IWAE},K}(x^{\mathrm{pre}}). (10.14)

It should be emphasized that both (10.13) and (10.14) are plug-in estimators. They are obtained by substituting unconditional estimators into the conditional identity, and they do not automatically inherit a lower-bound property from the unconditional estimators. Strictly speaking, they should therefore be interpreted as practical estimators of conditional log-likelihood.

For a block-causal prior, the conditional estimator can also be written in a blockwise form aligned with the architecture. Suppose the latent sequence is partitioned into prefix blocks and response blocks:

z=(z(1),…,z(B),z(B+1),…,z(B+R)).z=(z^{(1)},\dots,z^{(B)},z^{(B+1)},\dots,z^{(B+R)}). (10.15)

If the prior admits a block-level causal factorization, then

pψ​(z)=pψ​(z(1))​∏b=2B+Rpψ​(z(b)∣z(<b)).p_{\psi}(z)=p_{\psi}(z^{(1)})\prod_{b=2}^{B+R}p_{\psi}(z^{(b)}\mid z^{(<b)}). (10.16)

Conditioned on the prefix latent zpre:=z(1:B)z^{\mathrm{pre}}:=z^{(1:B)}, the conditional marginal of the response is

p​(xres∣xpre,zpre)=∫pθ​(xres∣xpre,zpre,zres)​pψ​(zres∣zpre)​dzres,p(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}},z^{\mathrm{pre}})=\int p_{\theta}(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}},z^{\mathrm{pre}},z^{\mathrm{res}})\,p_{\psi}(z^{\mathrm{res}}\mid z^{\mathrm{pre}})\,\mathrm{d}z^{\mathrm{res}}, (10.17)

where zres:=z(B+1:B+R)z^{\mathrm{res}}:=z^{(B+1:B+R)}. For any approximate posterior qϕ​(zres∣xpre,xres,zpre)q_{\phi}(z^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}},x^{\mathrm{res}},z^{\mathrm{pre}}), one has the conditional ELBO

log⁡p​(xres∣xpre,zpre)≥\displaystyle\log p(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}},z^{\mathrm{pre}})\geq Eqϕ​(zres∣xpre,xres,zpre)[logpθ(xres∣xpre,zpre,zres)\displaystyle E_{q_{\phi}(z^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}},x^{\mathrm{res}},z^{\mathrm{pre}})}\Bigl[\log p_{\theta}(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}},z^{\mathrm{pre}},z^{\mathrm{res}}) (10.18)
+logpψ(zres∣zpre)−logqϕ(zres∣xpre,xres,zpre)].\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\log p_{\psi}(z^{\mathrm{res}}\mid z^{\mathrm{pre}})-\log q_{\phi}(z^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}},x^{\mathrm{res}},z^{\mathrm{pre}})\Bigr]. (10.19)

Marginalizing over the true posterior of the prefix latent then yields

p​(xres∣xpre)=∫p​(xres∣xpre,zpre)​p​(zpre∣xpre)​dzpre.p(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}})=\int p(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}},z^{\mathrm{pre}})\,p(z^{\mathrm{pre}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}})\,\mathrm{d}z^{\mathrm{pre}}. (10.20)

Thus, a strict conditional probability requires not only marginalization over the response latent, but also an additional integration over the posterior uncertainty of the prefix latent. In practice, two approximations are common: one uses the joint-minus-prefix estimator in (10.12), while the other approximates p​(zpre∣xpre)p(z^{\mathrm{pre}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}}) with the encoder mean or a single encoder sample and then evaluates (10.19).

If the response contains only one new block, the above expression reduces to a single-block response score:

𝒮resp​(x(B+1);x(1:B),z(1:B)):=\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{resp}}(x^{(B+1)};x^{(1:B)},z^{(1:B)}):= Eqϕ​(z(B+1)∣x(1:B+1),z(1:B))[logpθ(x(B+1)∣x(1:B),z(1:B+1))\displaystyle E_{q_{\phi}(z^{(B+1)}\mid x^{(1:B+1)},z^{(1:B)})}\Bigl[\log p_{\theta}(x^{(B+1)}\mid x^{(1:B)},z^{(1:B+1)}) (10.21)
+logpψ(z(B+1)∣z(1:B))−logqϕ(z(B+1)∣x(1:B+1),z(1:B))].\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\log p_{\psi}(z^{(B+1)}\mid z^{(1:B)})-\log q_{\phi}(z^{(B+1)}\mid x^{(1:B+1)},z^{(1:B)})\Bigr]. (10.22)

This form is especially useful for scoring multiple-choice options, ranking candidate responses, and analyzing whether the separation between candidates is driven mainly by the prior term or the decoder term.

10.4 Numerical Evaluation of the CNF Prior and Estimation Algorithms

To evaluate log⁡pψ​(z0(k))\log p_{\psi}(z_{0}^{(k)}) in (10.8), one solves the augmented ODE

dd​t​[ztℓt]=[𝒗ψ​(zt,t)∇⋅𝒗ψ​(zt,t)],[z0ℓ0]=[z0(k)0].\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\begin{bmatrix}z_{t}\\ \ell_{t}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t)\\ \nabla\!\cdot\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t)\end{bmatrix},\qquad\begin{bmatrix}z_{0}\\ \ell_{0}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}z_{0}^{(k)}\\ 0\end{bmatrix}. (10.23)

Integrating from t=0t=0 to t=1t=1 gives (z1(k),ℓ1(k))(z_{1}^{(k)},\ell_{1}^{(k)}), and therefore

log⁡pψ​(z0(k))=log⁡p1​(z1(k))+ℓ1(k).\log p_{\psi}(z_{0}^{(k)})=\log p_{1}(z_{1}^{(k)})+\ell_{1}^{(k)}. (10.24)

In high dimensions, the divergence can be approximated by the Hutchinson trace estimator:

∇⋅𝒗ψ​(zt,t)=Tr​(∂𝒗ψ​(zt,t)∂zt)=𝔼ϵ​[ϵ⊤​∂𝒗ψ​(zt,t)∂zt​ϵ].\nabla\!\cdot\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t)=\mathrm{Tr}\!\left(\frac{\partial\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t)}{\partial z_{t}}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\epsilon}}\left[\bm{\epsilon}^{\top}\frac{\partial\bm{v}_{\psi}(z_{t},t)}{\partial z_{t}}\bm{\epsilon}\right]. (10.25)

In practice, one usually fixes the same random vector ϵ\bm{\epsilon} within a single ODE solve so that the induced dynamics remain consistent along that trajectory.

We now present two estimators corresponding to the above formulas. To avoid extra package dependencies, the algorithms are written in directly compilable pseudo-code style.

Algorithm A.1: Unconditional Log-Likelihood Estimation (ELBO / IWAE)

Input: sequence xx; encoder qϕq_{\phi}; decoder pθp_{\theta}; CNF prior pψp_{\psi}; sample number KK; estimation mode mode∈{ELBO,IWAE}\texttt{mode}\in\{\texttt{ELBO},\texttt{IWAE}\}.
Procedure:

  1. 1.

    For each k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K, sample z0(k)∼qϕ​(z0∣x)z_{0}^{(k)}\sim q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x).

  2. 2.

    Starting from (z0(k),0)(z_{0}^{(k)},0), solve (10.23) to t=1t=1 and obtain (z1(k),ℓ1(k))(z_{1}^{(k)},\ell_{1}^{(k)}).

  3. 3.

    Compute log⁡pψ​(z0(k))=log⁡p1​(z1(k))+ℓ1(k)\log p_{\psi}(z_{0}^{(k)})=\log p_{1}(z_{1}^{(k)})+\ell_{1}^{(k)}.

  4. 4.

    Compute log⁡pθ​(x∣z0(k))\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}^{(k)}) and log⁡qϕ​(z0(k)∣x)\log q_{\phi}(z_{0}^{(k)}\mid x).

  5. 5.

    Construct the importance weight

    log⁡w(k)←log⁡pθ​(x∣z0(k))+log⁡pψ​(z0(k))−log⁡qϕ​(z0(k)∣x).\log w^{(k)}\leftarrow\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}^{(k)})+\log p_{\psi}(z_{0}^{(k)})-\log q_{\phi}(z_{0}^{(k)}\mid x).
  6. 6.

    If mode=ELBO\texttt{mode}=\texttt{ELBO}, return

    log⁡p^​(x)=1K​∑k=1Klog⁡w(k);\widehat{\log p}(x)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log w^{(k)};

    otherwise return

    log⁡p^​(x)=log⁡(1K​∑k=1Kelog⁡w(k)).\widehat{\log p}(x)=\log\!\left(\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}e^{\log w^{(k)}}\right).

Output: an unconditional log-likelihood estimate log⁡p^​(x)\widehat{\log p}(x) for sequence xx.

Algorithm A.2: Conditional Log-Likelihood Estimation (Joint Minus Prefix)

Input: prefix xprex^{\mathrm{pre}}; response xresx^{\mathrm{res}}; sample number KK; estimation mode mode∈{ELBO,IWAE}\texttt{mode}\in\{\texttt{ELBO},\texttt{IWAE}\}.
Procedure:

  1. 1.

    Construct the full sequence xfull=(xpre,xres)x^{\mathrm{full}}=(x^{\mathrm{pre}},x^{\mathrm{res}}).

  2. 2.

    Call Algorithm A.1 to estimate log⁡p^​(xfull)\widehat{\log p}(x^{\mathrm{full}}).

  3. 3.

    Call Algorithm A.1 to estimate log⁡p^​(xpre)\widehat{\log p}(x^{\mathrm{pre}}).

  4. 4.

    Compute

    log⁡p^​(xres∣xpre)←log⁡p^​(xfull)−log⁡p^​(xpre).\widehat{\log p}(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}})\leftarrow\widehat{\log p}(x^{\mathrm{full}})-\widehat{\log p}(x^{\mathrm{pre}}).

Output: a conditional log-likelihood estimate log⁡p^​(xres∣xpre)\widehat{\log p}(x^{\mathrm{res}}\mid x^{\mathrm{pre}}).

Algorithm A.1 applies to both ELBO-style and IWAE-style estimators. Algorithm A.2 treats it as a black-box unconditional likelihood estimator and combines two calls through the conditional identity. If the task focuses only on the local score of a single newly generated block, then (10.22) can be used directly to rank candidate responses.

11 Comparison Under a Unified Markov Path View

This appendix further develops the mathematical comparison behind the main-text discussion of unified text modeling. The central question is not which method is more diffusion-like at a superficial level, but rather: into what state space and along what type of path does each method factorize the text distribution, and what role does that path play in generation?

11.1 A Unified Framework for Process-Based Generative Models

To establish a common language, consider the abstract definition of a process-based generative model. Let

Y=(Yt)t∈𝒯,Yt∈𝒮,Y=(Y_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{T}},\qquad Y_{t}\in\mathcal{S}, (11.1)

where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space and 𝒯\mathcal{T} is either discrete time or continuous time. If there exists a family of transition kernels

Kt←s​(d​yt∣ys),s≤t,K_{t\leftarrow s}(\mathrm{d}y_{t}\mid y_{s}),\qquad s\leq t, (11.2)

satisfying the Chapman–Kolmogorov relation, then YY forms a Markov process. If one additionally specifies an emission kernel

eθ​(x∣yt⋆),e_{\theta}(x\mid y_{t_{\star}}), (11.3)

then the text distribution can be written uniformly as

pθ​(x)=∫eθ​(x∣yt⋆)​pθ​(d​Y).p_{\theta}(x)=\int e_{\theta}(x\mid y_{t_{\star}})\,p_{\theta}(\mathrm{d}Y). (11.4)

Within this framework, the difference among AR, LLaDA, Plaid, and 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is not simply whether each admits a stepwise sampling algorithm. The essential distinction is that they factorize the text distribution over different state spaces and assign fundamentally different roles to the underlying paths. More specifically, they differ at least in the following six aspects: state space, state trajectory object, transition mechanism, the role of the path in generation, the point at which the observation is read out, and the tightness of the training objective relative to the true log-likelihood.

This unified view shows that the key question is not which method uses diffusion, but rather what type of distributional complexity is decomposed into what kind of path over what kind of state space, and whether that path is an observation-dependent corruption path or an observation-independent latent prior path.

11.2 Difference from Autoregressive Models: Why Diffusion

AR models text directly via the chain rule:

pηAR​(x)=∏i=1Lpη​(xi∣x<i).p_{\eta}^{\mathrm{AR}}(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{L}p_{\eta}(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}). (11.5)

Its negative log-likelihood is

−log⁡pηAR​(x)=∑i=1L−log⁡pη​(xi∣x<i).-\log p_{\eta}^{\mathrm{AR}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{L}-\log p_{\eta}(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}). (11.6)

The advantage of AR is therefore exact token-level likelihood and the most direct training and evaluation protocol. Its limitation comes from the fixed left-to-right conditioning order.

Under the unified path framework, AR can be written using prefix states

Si:=x1:i,S0:=∅.S_{i}:=x_{1:i},\qquad S_{0}:=\varnothing. (11.7)

Then (Si)i=0L(S_{i})_{i=0}^{L} forms a time-inhomogeneous Markov chain, whose one-step transition kernel is exactly the AR conditional distribution:

ℙ​(Si=si∣S0:i−1)=ℙ​(Si=si∣Si−1=si−1)=pη​(xi∣x<i).\mathbb{P}(S_{i}=s_{i}\mid S_{0:i-1})=\mathbb{P}(S_{i}=s_{i}\mid S_{i-1}=s_{i-1})=p_{\eta}(x_{i}\mid x_{<i}). (11.8)

Thus, the core inductive bias of AR is not merely Markovianity, but the fact that conditioning is restricted to the unique prefix filtration

σ​(X1)⊂σ​(X1:2)⊂⋯⊂σ​(X1:L).\sigma(X_{1})\subset\sigma(X_{1:2})\subset\cdots\subset\sigma(X_{1:L}). (11.9)

By contrast, the model distribution of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is not defined through a fixed token order, but by latent marginalization:

pCola​DLM​(x)=∫pθ​(x∣z0)​pψ​(z0)​dz0.p^{\mathrm{Cola\ DLM}}(x)=\int p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})\,p_{\psi}(z_{0})\,\mathrm{d}z_{0}. (11.10)

If the decoder itself is not left-to-right autoregressive, the resulting model distribution is not tied to any pre-specified token ordering. In this sense, the non-AR nature of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM comes from two levels: the prior pψ​(z0)p_{\psi}(z_{0}) is defined by continuous transport rather than token-wise chain factorization, and if the decoder is also non-AR, then generation becomes a two-stage procedure of first sampling global semantic latent variables and then realizing text conditionally.

From the optimization viewpoint, both families minimize

KL​(pdata​(x)∥pmodel​(x)),\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{model}}(x)\bigr), (11.11)

but they parameterize p​(x)p(x) differently. AR uses a chain-rule factorization, whereas 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM uses latent marginalization. Therefore, the strict meaning of why diffusion here is not to avoid maximum likelihood, but to improve the fit of pψ​(z0)p_{\psi}(z_{0}) to the aggregated posterior through a more expressive continuous prior family.

This can be quantified exactly. For any two candidate priors pap_{a} and pbp_{b},

𝔼q¯ϕ​(z0)​[log⁡pb​(z0)−log⁡pa​(z0)]=KL​(q¯ϕ​(z0)∥pa​(z0))−KL​(q¯ϕ​(z0)∥pb​(z0)).\mathbb{E}_{\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0})}[\log p_{b}(z_{0})-\log p_{a}(z_{0})]=\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0})\,\|\,p_{a}(z_{0})\bigr)-\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0})\,\|\,p_{b}(z_{0})\bigr). (11.12)

Hence, whenever the flow/CNF prior is closer to q¯ϕ​(z0)\bar{q}_{\phi}(z_{0}) than a simple Gaussian prior, it improves the average ELBO.

11.3 Difference from Discrete Denoising Language Models: Why Continuous

Discrete denoising language models such as LLaDA operate directly in token space. A typical training objective can be written as

ℒMDM​(θ):=𝔼t∼U​[0,1],x0,xt​[1t​∑i=1L𝟏​[xti=M]​(−log⁡pθ​(x0i∣xt))],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MDM}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim U[0,1],\,x_{0},\,x_{t}}\left[\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\mathbf{1}[x_{t}^{i}=M]\bigl(-\log p_{\theta}(x_{0}^{i}\mid x_{t})\bigr)\right], (11.13)

and satisfies

−𝔼pdata​(x0)​log⁡pθ​(x0)≤ℒMDM​(θ).-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_{0})}\log p_{\theta}(x_{0})\leq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MDM}}(\theta). (11.14)

Thus, LLaDA learns a token-space distribution through reverse recovery under random mask ratios. Its advantage is that it has no explicit encoder and no latent bottleneck; its limitation is that it always remains in a discrete state space.

More precisely, the forward masking process of LLaDA can be embedded into a continuous-time Markov chain. For a single token, let the state space be 𝒱∪{M}\mathcal{V}\cup\{M\} and define the generator

Gτ​(a,M)=λ​(τ),Gτ​(a,a)=−λ​(τ),Gτ​(M,M)=0,G_{\tau}(a,M)=\lambda(\tau),\qquad G_{\tau}(a,a)=-\lambda(\tau),\qquad G_{\tau}(M,M)=0, (11.15)

where a∈𝒱a\in\mathcal{V}. Then the transition probability from any non-mask state to the absorbing mask state is

ℙ​(Xτ=M∣X0=a)=1−exp⁡(−∫0τλ​(u)​du).\mathbb{P}(X_{\tau}=M\mid X_{0}=a)=1-\exp\Bigl(-\int_{0}^{\tau}\lambda(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\Bigr). (11.16)

If the right-hand side is identified with t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], one recovers the forward kernel in which each token is masked with probability tt, as used in (11.13). Therefore, LLaDA can be understood rigorously as a reverse recovery problem over a CTMC with discrete states and absorption into the mask state.

By contrast, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM models pψ​(z0)p_{\psi}(z_{0}) in continuous latent space rather than performing discrete diffusion in token space. This continuous formulation provides three strict advantages. First, continuous-time change-of-variables yields an explicit log-density, namely (9.13). Second, vector-field regression in Euclidean space allows the use of Flow Matching to learn prior geometry directly. Third, continuous latent variables naturally support interpolation, gradient guidance, and representation editing.

Accordingly, the meaning of why continuous is not that continuous representations are inherently superior to discrete ones. Rather, compared with a discrete token-space corruption model, continuous latent space permits a more direct description of probability geometry and reversible transport. Whether this yields actual gains still depends on whether the continuous structure aligns with the low-dimensional semantic organization of the data.

11.4 Difference from Plaid: Why Latent

Plaid is also a continuous method, but it makes continuous a token-aligned representation that stays close to the original sequence, rather than an explicit semantic latent variable. A typical forward process can be written as

q​(h0∣x)=𝒩​(x~,σ2​(0)​I),q​(ht∣hs)=𝒩​(hs,σ2​(t)−σ2​(s)),q(h_{0}\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{x},\sigma^{2}(0)I),\qquad q(h_{t}\mid h_{s})=\mathcal{N}\bigl(h_{s},\sigma^{2}(t)-\sigma^{2}(s)\bigr), (11.17)

where x~=Embed​(x)\widetilde{x}=\mathrm{Embed}(x). Hence, as the noise level approaches zero, the state of Plaid still remains tightly attached to the observation space. By contrast, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM explicitly separates global semantic representation from textual realization through

p​(x)=∫pθ​(x∣z0)​pψ​(z0)​dz0.p(x)=\int p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})p_{\psi}(z_{0})\,\mathrm{d}z_{0}. (11.18)

This distinction is not merely about where continuity is introduced; it is about how the model is factorized. If one further lets

qϕ​(z0∣x)=𝒩​(E​(x),σ02​I),σ02→0,q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(E(x),\sigma_{0}^{2}I),\qquad\sigma_{0}^{2}\to 0, (11.19)

and E​(x)E(x) is nearly invertible, then 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM degenerates to the limiting case where z0z_{0} is almost just a continuousized representation of the original sequence. This limit clarifies the structural relation: Plaid is closer to the near-observation, non-compressive limit of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM, while the genuinely new ingredient of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is the latent decomposition itself.

The mathematical core of this difference is captured by the information decomposition of the average ELBO in (9.28). That decomposition shows that representation learning in 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM splits into three parts: the conditional reconstruction term controls textual realization given the latent, the mutual information Iq​(X;Z0)I_{q}(X;Z_{0}) controls how much global information about the text is retained, and the KL between the aggregated posterior and the prior controls the difficulty of prior matching. Precisely because this explicit latent variable is introduced, the model can encode global planning, topic, and style constraints into z0z_{0}, while delegating local token realization to the decoder.

Therefore, the strict answer to why latent is that a latent variable is not merely a continuous relaxation of a discrete object. It is an intermediate random variable that explicitly participates in marginalization, allowing the text generation problem to be decomposed into prior modeling plus conditional realization. This decomposition yields statistical benefits only when the data indeed contain low-rate but high-value semantic structure; this issue is analyzed further in Appendix 12.

11.5 Why Cola DLM Is Not Merely a Latent Reverse-Diffusion LM

To avoid conceptual confusion, we now make the distinction more precise. Suppose a narrow latent diffusion LM is defined as follows: one first specifies a data-conditioned forward noising process on a latent state,

q​(z0:T∣x),q(z_{0:T}\mid x), (11.20)

and then learns its reverse process to gradually recover a latent state used for text generation. The core structure of such a model is therefore the reversal of a data-conditioned forward corruption process.

Under this narrow definition, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is not simply a latent reverse-diffusion LM. First, the continuous path in 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM lies in prior transport:

z1∼p1​(z1),z0=Φ0←1ψ​(z1),x∼pθ​(x∣z0).z_{1}\sim p_{1}(z_{1}),\qquad z_{0}=\Phi^{\psi}_{0\leftarrow 1}(z_{1}),\qquad x\sim p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}). (11.21)

This path first describes how to generate a semantic prior sample in latent space from a simple Gaussian. During generation, it does not depend on any specific observation xx. By contrast, the forward paths in Plaid and LLaDA describe how a given sample xx is perturbed into a high-noise state. Thus, although all three can be described as path models, the path in 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is prior transport, whereas the paths in Plaid and LLaDA are data corruption.

Second, in 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM the encoder appears only in variational inference:

log⁡p​(x)≥𝔼qϕ​(z0∣x)​[log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)+log⁡pψ​(z0)−log⁡qϕ​(z0∣x)].\log p(x)\geq\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)}\Bigl[\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})+\log p_{\psi}(z_{0})-\log q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\Bigr]. (11.22)

It does not participate in the generation procedure (11.21), and is therefore part of the variational posterior. In Plaid and LLaDA, however, the forward process qq is part of the model definition because the reverse model is trained against that corruption law. In short, the former qq belongs to inference, whereas the latter qq belongs to model construction.

Finally, the marginal distribution of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is always defined by the hierarchical latent-variable identity

p​(x)=∫pθ​(x∣z0)​pψ​(z0)​dz0.p(x)=\int p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})p_{\psi}(z_{0})\,\mathrm{d}z_{0}. (11.23)

Strictly speaking, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is therefore first and foremost a hierarchical latent-variable language model with a CNF prior. Flow or diffusion is only a way to make the prior family more expressive, not the entirety of the model itself.

12 Theoretical Advantages, Applicability, and Limitations

We finally compare 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM with AR, LLaDA, and Plaid under a unified theoretical criterion. The goal is not to argue that a more complex model should be stronger, but to ask under what conditions 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is expected to be better, and under what conditions it is expected to be worse.

12.1 A Unified Population-Level Comparison Criterion

For any model class ℳ\mathcal{M}, define its irreducible approximation error with respect to the true data distribution pdata​(x)p_{\mathrm{data}}(x) as

ℰ​(ℳ):=infp∈ℳKL​(pdata​(x)∥p​(x)).\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{M}):=\inf_{p\in\mathcal{M}}\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)\,\|\,p(x)\bigr). (12.1)

This quantity measures the best unavoidable mismatch of the model class even after ignoring finite-sample effects and optimization error.

For any model trained by exact negative log-likelihood, one has the standard identity

infp∈ℳ𝔼pdata​(x)​[−log⁡p​(x)]=H​(pdata)+ℰ​(ℳ),\inf_{p\in\mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}[-\log p(x)]=H(p_{\mathrm{data}})+\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{M}), (12.2)

where H​(pdata):=−𝔼pdata​(x)​log⁡pdata​(x)H(p_{\mathrm{data}}):=-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(x) is the data entropy. Therefore, for exact-NLL models, comparing theoretical limits is equivalent to comparing ℰ​(ℳ)\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{M}).

AR belongs to this class, and its population risk is

𝔼pdata​(x)​[−log⁡pηAR​(x)]=H​(pdata)+KL​(pdata∥pηAR).\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}[-\log p^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\eta}(x)]=H(p_{\mathrm{data}})+\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{data}}\,\|\,p^{\mathrm{AR}}_{\eta}\bigr). (12.3)

By contrast, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is trained through the ELBO, so for each sample

−ℒELBO(x)=−logpθ,ψ(x)+KL(qϕ(z0∣x)∥pθ,ψ(z0∣x)).-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)=-\log p_{\theta,\psi}(x)+\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\,\|\,p_{\theta,\psi}(z_{0}\mid x)\bigr). (12.4)

Taking expectation over the data distribution gives

𝔼pdata​(x)​[−ℒELBO​(x)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}[-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)] =H​(pdata)+KL​(pdata∥pθ,ψ)+𝒢Cola​DLMinfer​(ϕ,θ,ψ),\displaystyle=H(p_{\mathrm{data}})+\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{data}}\,\|\,p_{\theta,\psi}\bigr)+\mathcal{G}^{\mathrm{infer}}_{\mathrm{Cola\ DLM}}(\phi,\theta,\psi), (12.5)

where

𝒢Cola​DLMinfer(ϕ,θ,ψ):=𝔼pdata​(x)KL(qϕ(z0∣x)∥pθ,ψ(z0∣x))≥0\mathcal{G}^{\mathrm{infer}}_{\mathrm{Cola\ DLM}}(\phi,\theta,\psi):=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\,\|\,p_{\theta,\psi}(z_{0}\mid x)\bigr)\geq 0 (12.6)

is the inference gap.

Similarly, the variational objective of Plaid can be written as true NLL plus a reverse/path-posterior gap, and the mask-denoising objective of LLaDA can be written as true token-space NLL plus a surrogate gap. Hence all four model classes can be unified as

population risk=H​(pdata)+model mismatch+additional gap induced by the training objective.\text{population risk}=H(p_{\mathrm{data}})+\text{model mismatch}+\text{additional gap induced by the training objective}. (12.7)

Therefore, theoretical superiority does not follow from model complexity alone. It depends on whether the total statistical burden is smaller.

Define the total statistical burden of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM as

ℜCola​DLM:=ℰ​(ℳCola​DLM)+infϕ,θ,ψ𝒢Cola​DLMinfer​(ϕ,θ,ψ),\mathfrak{R}_{\mathrm{Cola\ DLM}}:=\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Cola\ DLM}})+\inf_{\phi,\theta,\psi}\mathcal{G}^{\mathrm{infer}}_{\mathrm{Cola\ DLM}}(\phi,\theta,\psi), (12.8)

and define analogous quantities for AR, Plaid, and LLaDA. Then, at the population level, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is better than a comparison class if and only if its total statistical burden is smaller. For example,

ℜCola​DLM<ℜAR⇔𝒞​o​l​a DLM is better than AR at the population level.\mathfrak{R}_{\mathrm{Cola\ DLM}}<\mathfrak{R}_{\mathrm{AR}}\iff\text{$\mathcal{C}ola$ {DLM} is better than AR at the population level}. (12.9)

This gives a unified and rigorous comparison criterion.

12.2 Rate-Distortion and the Applicability Boundary of the Latent Bottleneck

The unified criterion still leaves a deeper question unanswered: why can latent decomposition reduce model mismatch in some cases but hurt modeling in others? The answer comes from conditional entropy, mutual information, and rate-distortion structure.

For any encoder qϕ​(z0∣x)q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x) and decoder pθ​(x∣z0)p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}), under the joint distribution q​(x,z0)=pdata​(x)​qϕ​(z0∣x)q(x,z_{0})=p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x) one always has

𝔼q​(x,z0)​[−log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)]≥Hq​(X∣Z0).\mathbb{E}_{q(x,z_{0})}[-\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})]\geq H_{q}(X\mid Z_{0}). (12.10)

By the mutual-information identity

Hq​(X)=Hq​(X∣Z0)+Iq​(X;Z0),H_{q}(X)=H_{q}(X\mid Z_{0})+I_{q}(X;Z_{0}), (12.11)

together with q​(x)=pdata​(x)q(x)=p_{\mathrm{data}}(x), it follows that

Hq​(X∣Z0)=H​(pdata)−Iq​(X;Z0).H_{q}(X\mid Z_{0})=H(p_{\mathrm{data}})-I_{q}(X;Z_{0}). (12.12)

Therefore, the reconstruction cost satisfies

𝔼q​(x,z0)​[−log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)]≥H​(pdata)−Iq​(X;Z0).\mathbb{E}_{q(x,z_{0})}[-\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})]\geq H(p_{\mathrm{data}})-I_{q}(X;Z_{0}). (12.13)

This shows that if Iq​(X;Z0)I_{q}(X;Z_{0}) is small, then the latent retains little information about the text and the lower bound on the best achievable reconstruction loss rises. If Iq​(X;Z0)I_{q}(X;Z_{0}) is large enough, then the decoder can realize the text more easily given the latent.

To formalize this further, define the representation rate-distortion function

𝒟​(R):=infq​(z0∣x):Iq​(X;Z0)≤Rinfpθ​(x∣z0)𝔼q​(x,z0)​[−log⁡pθ​(x∣z0)].\mathcal{D}(R):=\inf_{q(z_{0}\mid x):\,I_{q}(X;Z_{0})\leq R}\ \inf_{p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})}\mathbb{E}_{q(x,z_{0})}[-\log p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0})]. (12.14)

It represents the minimum achievable average reconstruction cost when the latent channel is allowed to transmit at most RR nats of information about the text.

If, for a given data distribution, 𝒟​(R)\mathcal{D}(R) falls quickly to a low level already at small RR, then the data admit a low-rate but high-value latent representation, and a latent bottleneck is more likely to help. If substantial reduction in reconstruction error occurs only when RR approaches H​(X)H(X), then the data are nearly incompressible and a latent bottleneck is more likely to become an additional burden.

Therefore, whether 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM benefits from the bottleneck is ultimately governed by the rate-distortion curve of the data itself. If global topics, plans, style, and constraints occupy a relatively low information rate yet strongly determine the final realization, then encoding them into z0z_{0} is efficient. If nearly every token-level detail is irreducible, then latent compression does not bring genuine statistical benefit.

12.3 Structured Generation Regime: When Cola DLM Better Matches the True Mechanism

To formalize the above intuition one step further, consider the following structured generation assumption: there exists a global variable GG such that the true data distribution can be written as

pdata​(x)=∫p⋆​(x∣g)​p⋆​(g)​dg,p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)=\int p^{\star}(x\mid g)\,p^{\star}(g)\,\mathrm{d}g, (12.15)

where GG determines topic, plan, discourse structure, style, or other global constraints, and p⋆​(x∣g)p^{\star}(x\mid g) realizes these global factors into concrete text. If, in addition,

H​(X∣G)≪H​(X),dim(G)≪dim(E​(X)),H(X\mid G)\ll H(X),\qquad\dim(G)\ll\dim(E(X)), (12.16)

then the data are in a favorable regime dominated by low-dimensional but high-value latent factors.

In this regime, the inductive bias of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is better aligned with the true generation mechanism. The encoder recovers posterior information about GG from xx, the prior learns a global semantic distribution close to p⋆​(g)p^{\star}(g), and the decoder learns textual realization conditioned on the global factor. In other words, the potential advantage of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM does not come from being more complicated, but from splitting a hard problem into two better-matched subproblems:

learning ​pdata​(x)↝learning ​p⋆​(g)​ and ​p⋆​(x∣g).\text{learning }p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)\quad\leadsto\quad\text{learning }p^{\star}(g)\text{ and }p^{\star}(x\mid g). (12.17)

If the encoder can recover information about GG with a small inference gap, pψ​(z0)p_{\psi}(z_{0}) can approximate the aggregated latent distribution corresponding to GG, and pθ​(x∣z0)p_{\theta}(x\mid z_{0}) can approximate the conditional realization well, then the statistical burden of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is determined primarily by the modeling complexity of the low-dimensional global factor rather than that of the full surface sequence. This is the fundamental source of its possible advantage over AR, LLaDA, and Plaid.

12.4 Three Curves, Theoretical Advantages, and Limitations

In the opposite regime, where (12.16) does not hold, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM may systematically underperform more direct modeling routes. Typical unfavorable cases include the absence of a low-rate sufficient representation, settings where local surface form itself carries the main semantics, or regimes where a strong token-space model is already adequate. In such cases, the additional costs of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM mainly come from three sources:

(i) inference gap ​𝒢Cola​DLMinfer,\displaystyle\text{inference gap }\mathcal{G}^{\mathrm{infer}}_{\mathrm{Cola\ DLM}}, (12.18)
(ii) the elevated reconstruction lower bound ​H​(X∣Z0)\displaystyle\text{the elevated reconstruction lower bound }H(X\mid Z_{0})
induced by the bottleneck,\displaystyle\text{induced by the bottleneck},
(iii) the optimization complexity of jointly training encoder,
prior, and decoder.\displaystyle\text{prior, and decoder}.

Hence, the success or failure of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM can be reduced to a competition among three curves: the representation rate-distortion curve 𝒟​(R)\mathcal{D}(R), the prior-approximation curve, and the inference-gap curve 𝒢Cola​DLMinfer\mathcal{G}^{\mathrm{infer}}_{\mathrm{Cola\ DLM}}. Only when all three favor 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM does latent decomposition become a true theoretical advantage.

These conclusions can be summarized more directly as follows.

Theoretical Advantages. Relative to AR, if the decoder is non-autoregressive, then 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM is not constrained by a single left-to-right ordering and can determine global semantics in latent space before realizing text, which gives it a potentially more natural inductive bias for infilling, constraint satisfaction, and global planning. Relative to discrete DLMs, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM has the geometric structure of continuous latent space and therefore supports explicit log-densities, vector-field regression, interpolation, and latent editing. Relative to Plaid, 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM explicitly introduces semantic compression, allowing the model to learn a low-dimensional global representation. If the data indeed exhibit a hierarchical structure of low-dimensional global semantics and high-dimensional local realization, this inductive bias is closer to the true mechanism. Finally, the information decomposition of the average ELBO makes it natural to analyze the representation, prior, and decoder as separate components.

Theoretical Limitations. 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM inherently suffers from a variational gap:

logp(x)−ℒELBO(x)=KL(qϕ(z0∣x)∥p(z0∣x)).\log p(x)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)=\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q_{\phi}(z_{0}\mid x)\,\|\,p(z_{0}\mid x)\bigr). (12.19)

If the encoder is poor, the model pays a systematic likelihood penalty. The latent bottleneck also introduces the risk of posterior collapse: if the decoder is too strong, the latent dimension is too small, or the regularization is too strong, then Iq​(X;Z0)I_{q}(X;Z_{0}) may become too small and the encoder may stop transmitting useful information. In addition, accurate evaluation of log⁡pψ​(z0)\log p_{\psi}(z_{0}) often requires ODE integration and divergence estimation, making evaluation more expensive than in AR models. Importantly, the potential advantage of 𝒞​o​l​a\mathcal{C}ola DLM does not follow automatically from using latent variables and flows. It relies on the inductive assumption that the data contain a favorable low-dimensional semantic latent structure. This requires experiments to verify.

13 Existence of Global Semantic Structures

The goal of this section is to establish a falsifiable null hypothesis and, based on it, show that if the latent representation consists only of purely local and separable components, then the optimal timestep shift should not exhibit a systematic drift as the latent dimension varies. We then compare the experimentally observed shift drift against this null hypothesis, thereby obtaining a more robust conclusion regarding the existence of shared structures. To avoid conflating conclusions that can be established rigorously with structural models introduced for interpretation, we first formulate an abstract null hypothesis.

Assumption 13.1 (Null hypothesis of purely separable representations).

Let dd denote the latent dimension, let δ\delta denote the timestep shift, and let 𝒥d​(δ)\mathcal{J}_{d}(\delta) denote the overall performance objective under a fixed semantic metric at latent dimension dd. Assume that the following conditions hold:

  1. 1.

    Local separability: there is no cross-dimensional joint structure in the latent representation that affects semantics, and the overall semantic performance is obtained by independently aggregating the contributions of local dimensions;

  2. 2.

    Homogeneity: each local dimension shares the same optimal temporal scale with respect to shift; changing dd only changes the number of independent dimensions and does not alter the functional form of each local subproblem;

  3. 3.

    Additive aggregation: the overall objective can be written as

    𝒥d​(δ)=∑i=1dji​(δ)or𝒥d​(δ)=1d​∑i=1dji​(δ),\mathcal{J}_{d}(\delta)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}j_{i}(\delta)\qquad\text{or}\qquad\mathcal{J}_{d}(\delta)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}j_{i}(\delta), (13.1)

    where all jij_{i} attain their optimum at the same point. More strongly, if homogeneity holds exactly, then there exists a common function jj and constants ad>0,bda_{d}>0,b_{d} such that

    𝒥d​(δ)=ad​j​(δ)+bd.\mathcal{J}_{d}(\delta)=a_{d}\,j(\delta)+b_{d}. (13.2)

Assumption 13.1 does not presuppose any specific network architecture. Rather, it describes a theoretical limit in which semantics is carried entirely by mutually independent local dimensions. Under this limit, changing the latent dimension can at most modify the scale of the overall objective, but should not change the location of the optimal shift.

Proposition 13.2 (Dimension-invariance of the optimal shift under the separable null).

Under Assumption 13.1, let

δd⋆∈arg⁡maxδ⁡𝒥d​(δ)\delta_{d}^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\delta}\mathcal{J}_{d}(\delta)

denote the optimal timestep shift at latent dimension dd. Then for any two dimensions d1,d2d_{1},d_{2}, we have

arg⁡maxδ⁡𝒥d1​(δ)=arg⁡maxδ⁡𝒥d2​(δ).\arg\max_{\delta}\mathcal{J}_{d_{1}}(\delta)=\arg\max_{\delta}\mathcal{J}_{d_{2}}(\delta). (13.3)

In particular, if the maximizer is unique, then

δd1⋆=δd2⋆.\delta_{d_{1}}^{\star}=\delta_{d_{2}}^{\star}. (13.4)

Therefore, under purely local and separable representations, the optimal timestep shift should not drift systematically with the latent dimension.

Proof.

By (13.2), for any dd,

𝒥d​(δ)=ad​j​(δ)+bd,ad>0.\mathcal{J}_{d}(\delta)=a_{d}\,j(\delta)+b_{d},\qquad a_{d}>0.

Since bdb_{d} is independent of δ\delta and ada_{d} only induces a positive rescaling, it follows that

arg⁡maxδ⁡𝒥d​(δ)=arg⁡maxδ⁡j​(δ).\arg\max_{\delta}\mathcal{J}_{d}(\delta)=\arg\max_{\delta}j(\delta).

Hence the optimal point is independent of dd, which proves (13.3) and (13.4). ∎

The key conclusion of Proposition 13.2 is that what can be established rigorously is that if no shared or joint structure affecting semantics exists, then the optimal shift should not drift systematically with the latent dimension.

Corollary 13.3 (Systematic drift refutes the purely separable null).

If experiments show that, as the latent dimension dd varies, the optimal shift δ⋆​(d)\delta^{\star}(d) exhibits a stable, monotonic, and reproducible systematic drift, and if this drift cannot be explained by changes in parameter count, insufficient training, optimization instability, or evaluation noise, then Assumption 13.1 does not hold.

Proof.

By Proposition 13.2, if Assumption 13.1 holds, then the optimal shift must be identical across all latent dimensions. If experiments repeatedly show that the optimal shift drifts systematically with dd, then this contradicts the necessary consequence of the null hypothesis. Therefore, the null hypothesis is rejected. ∎

The boundary of the conclusion in Corollary 13.3 is clear: it directly rules out the hypothesis that the latent space is purely local and separable. Consequently, the strictly derivable conclusion is that some cross-dimensional shared or joint structure must exist in the latent representation. If one further wishes to interpret this structure as a global semantic factor, additional modeling assumptions and experimental evidence are required.

An equivalent formulation from an information-theoretic perspective

The above conclusion admits a consistent restatement in information-theoretic terms. Let ss denote a latent variable associated with high-level semantics, and let zz denote the VAE latent. Then the diffusion forward process can be written as

zt=αt​z+σt​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩​(0,I),z_{t}=\alpha_{t}z+\sigma_{t}\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), (13.5)

where αt\alpha_{t} and σt\sigma_{t} are determined by the noise schedule. If we further decompose the latent as

z=ϕ​(s)+u,z=\phi(s)+u, (13.6)

where ϕ​(s)\phi(s) denotes the effective signal induced by the semantic variable and uu denotes encoding residuals or posterior uncertainty, then the observation received by the DiT at timestep tt becomes

zt=αt​ϕ​(s)+αt​u+σt​ϵ⏟total noise.z_{t}=\alpha_{t}\phi(s)+\underbrace{\alpha_{t}u+\sigma_{t}\epsilon}_{\text{total noise}}. (13.7)

Hence, what matters to the DiT is not the raw timestep itself, but rather how much effective information about ss is still preserved in the latent at that timestep.

Under Assumption 13.1, if semantics is carried entirely by local independent dimensions, namely

s=(s1,…,sd),z=(z1,…,zd),s=(s_{1},\dots,s_{d}),\qquad z=(z_{1},\dots,z_{d}),

and if the channels are independent and identically distributed across dimensions, then the additivity of mutual information yields

I​(s;zt)=∑i=1dI​(si;zt,i).I(s;z_{t})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}I(s_{i};z_{t,i}). (13.8)
